title: systemd, journalctl and cron
summary: Run programs as services that restart themselves, read their logs, and schedule jobs.

steps.title: Services with systemd
body: A **service** is a program systemd starts at boot, restarts when it crashes, and logs for you. It's described by a **unit file**:

steps.prompt: Match the systemctl command to its effect.
pairs: state, PID and the last log lines
re-read unit files after editing them

steps.prompt: You edited `orders-api.service`. Arrange the steps to apply and verify the change.
steps.explain: systemd caches unit files, so reload first. Then restart, check status, and read recent logs to be sure.

steps.title: Logs with journalctl
body: systemd captures each service's stdout and stderr into the **journal**.
journalctl -p err -b                   # errors (and worse) since this boot
Priorities, most to least severe: `emerg alert crit err warning notice info debug`. `-p err` means err **or more severe**.

steps.prompt: Follow the orders-api logs, starting with the last 20 lines.
steps.explain: `-u` picks the unit, `-n` the number of lines, `-f` follows.

steps.prompt: `systemctl status orders-api` shows `Active: activating (auto-restart)` and `code=exited, status=150`. What's the next thing to run?
options: `journalctl -u orders-api -n 50` to read why it exits
steps.explain: It's crash-looping under `Restart=on-failure`. The program's own error message (bad config, port taken, missing file) is in the journal.

steps.title: cron: run on a schedule
body: `crontab -e` edits your schedule. Each line is five time fields and a command:
│ │ │ │ ┌ day of week  0-7 (0 and 7 are Sunday)

cron runs with a minimal `PATH` and in your home directory: use absolute paths and redirect output (`>> /var/log/backup.log 2>&1`), or you'll never see the errors. (systemd **timers** are the modern alternative.)

steps.prompt: When does `0 */6 * * *` run? List the times on one line, separated by spaces.
steps.explain: `*/6` in the hour field means every 6th hour starting from 0; minute 0 each time.

steps.prompt: Does the cron line `0 9 * * 1-5` fire at this time?

steps.title: Fix a crontab, then write a timer
prompt: `~/jobs.cron` is the crontab a colleague wants installed, but `crontab ~/jobs.cron` refuses it. Fix and install it,
then move the backup to a systemd timer.
1. Fix `~/jobs.cron`: `rotate.sh` should run **every 15 minutes**, and the `tar` line must work under cron (look at
what cron does with `%`). Install it with `crontab ~/jobs.cron` and check with `crontab -l`.
2. Write `~/units/backup.timer` for the existing `~/units/backup.service`: run it at **02:30 on weekdays**, catch up
after downtime (`Persistent=true`), and enable it under `timers.target`. `systemd-analyze calendar` and
`systemd-analyze verify` (both work here) tell you whether systemd agrees.

checks.name: a crontab is installed
checks.fail: No crontab is installed. `crontab ~/jobs.cron` installs the file (and refuses it while it has errors).

checks.name: the backup line is still there
checks.fail: The weekday 02:30 backup line is missing from `crontab -l`.

checks.name: rotate.sh runs every 15 minutes
checks.fail: The `rotate.sh` line should start `*/15 * * * *`. Minutes go from 0 to 59, so `61` is what `crontab` called a *bad minute*.

checks.name: the % in the tar line is escaped
checks.fail: In a crontab, an unescaped `%` ends the command (the rest becomes its input). Write `date +\%F`.

checks.name: the timer fires at 02:30 on weekdays
checks.fail: `systemd-analyze calendar` does not normalise your `OnCalendar=` to `Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00`. Try `OnCalendar=Mon..Fri 02:30`.

checks.name: the timer is enabled under timers.target
systemd-analyze verify accepts it
checks.fail: `systemd-analyze verify ~/units/backup.timer` reports a problem: read its message.

hints: Run `crontab ~/jobs.cron` and read the error: it names the line. Minutes are 0-59; every 15 minutes is `*/15`.
Cron turns `%` into a newline. `sed -i 's/+%F/+\\%F/' ~/jobs.cron` escapes it. Then `crontab ~/jobs.cron && crontab -l`.
explain: On a real server the timer goes into `/etc/systemd/system/` next to its service, then `systemctl daemon-reload` and
`systemctl enable --now backup.timer`; `systemctl list-timers` shows the next run. Timers log to the journal, can
catch up after downtime (`Persistent=true`), spread load with `RandomizedDelaySec=`, and never hit the `%` trap.
That is why new jobs on systemd machines are usually timers. Cron is still everywhere, so read both.

steps.title: Mission: cron and automation
prompt: Robots should do the boring jobs. In **Cron and automation**, do **Every five minutes**: write a real crontab line and let the lab check it.
steps.explain: `*/5 * * * *` means every five minutes. Under cron the PATH is tiny and there is no terminal: use full paths and send output to a log.
